19.text: A cloudburst is conceptually linked to rapid-onset disasters.
Heavy rainfall can contribute to flooding.

Flood management includes flood forecasting, warnings, and disaster preparedness.
Poor drainage aggravates urban flooding.

Poor planning aggravates urban flooding.
The IMD defines a cloudburst as extremely intense rainfall over an area of approximately 20–30 square kilometres.
The IMD definition of a cloudburst requires rainfall of at least 100 mm (10 cm) in one hour.
A cloudburst is a highly localised extreme weather event.
A cloudburst is a short-duration extreme weather event.
A cloudburst is often accompanied by thunderstorms.
A cloudburst can trigger flash floods.
A cloudburst can trigger landslides.
Cloudbursts mostly occur at altitudes between 1,000 and 2,500 metres in mountainous regions.
Orographic lifting occurs when warm, moist air is forced to rise rapidly over steep mountain slopes.
Atmospheric instability produces strong convection and towering cumulonimbus clouds.
High moisture availability in monsoon air masses contributes to cloudbursts.
A sudden release occurs when updrafts weaken and accumulated water falls intensively.
The Himalayan region includes Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, and Sikkim as vulnerable cloudburst-prone areas.
Steep slopes contribute to the vulnerability of the Himalayan region to cloudbursts.
The orographic effect contributes to the vulnerability of the Himalayan region to cloudbursts.
The monsoon contributes to the vulnerability of the Himalayan region to cloudbursts.
The Western Ghats include parts of Kerala, Karnataka, and Maharashtra as areas vulnerable to cloudbursts.
Intense monsoon rainfall on the windward side contributes to the vulnerability of the Western Ghats.
Cloudbursts occasionally occur in plains, although such events are rare.
Localised convection contributes to occasional cloudbursts in plains.
The main cloudburst trigger mechanism is the orographic lifting of moist air.
Flash floods and landslides are major secondary hazards of cloudbursts.
Forecasting cloudbursts is extremely difficult because of their highly localised nature.

Nowcasting is a key cloudburst forecasting tool.

10.text: An earthquake is a geological disaster.
An earthquake is not an atmospheric natural disaster.
The focus is the origin point inside Earth.
The epicentre is the point directly above the focus on the surface.
Earthquake intensity is measured using the Mercalli Scale.
A seismograph is used to measure earthquake intensity.
India has four seismic zones.
Andhra Pradesh lies in Seismic Zone II and Seismic Zone III.
Seismic Zone V has very high risk.
Seismic Zone V has an expected intensity of IX and above on the MSK scale.
The zone factor of Seismic Zone V is 0.36.
Seismic Zone V covers the entire North-East, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, parts of Bihar, Kutch in Gujarat, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Seismic Zone IV has high risk.
Seismic Zone IV has an expected intensity of VIII on the MSK scale.
The zone factor of Seismic Zone IV is 0.24.
Seismic Zone IV covers Delhi, parts of Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh, North Bihar, parts of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra.
Seismic Zone III has moderate risk.
Seismic Zone III has an expected intensity of VII on the MSK scale.
The zone factor of Seismic Zone III is 0.16.
Seismic Zone III covers the remaining Indo-Gangetic plains, coastal areas, Kerala, Goa, and parts of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.
Seismic Zone II has low risk.
Seismic Zone II has an expected intensity of VI or less on the MSK scale.
The zone factor of Seismic Zone II is 0.10.
Seismic Zone II covers most of Peninsular India, which is a stable region.
